cards.statement: Assigning an IAM Identity Center permission set provisions an IAM role in the target AWS account.
cards.explanation: IAM Identity Center implements account access by creating and managing a role whose policies reflect the assigned permission set.

source.title: Manage AWS accounts with permission sets

cards.statement: Applications can use AWS STS AssumeRole to obtain long-term credentials for cross-account access.
cards.explanation: AssumeRole returns temporary security credentials with an expiration time. Applications need refreshed credentials after those credentials expire.
cards.misconception: Assuming a cross-account role creates permanent programmatic credentials.

source.title: AssumeRole

cards.statement: An identity-based Allow can override an applicable explicit Deny in an AWS resource-based policy.
cards.explanation: An applicable explicit Deny takes precedence over an Allow during IAM policy evaluation, including when the policies are of different types.
cards.misconception: Identity-based permissions take priority over explicit resource-based denials.

source.title: Policy evaluation logic

cards.statement: An Allow in an AWS Organizations service control policy grants that action to member-account users.
cards.explanation: Service control policies define an organization's permission ceiling. An allowed action still needs a separate grant from an applicable permissions policy.
cards.misconception: A service control policy can directly grant permissions to IAM identities.

source.title: Service control policies (SCPs)

cards.statement: An IAM permissions boundary caps the permissions that identity-based policies can grant to its attached role.
cards.explanation: For a role with a permissions boundary, an identity-based permission must be allowed by both the identity policy and the boundary.

source.title: Permissions boundaries for IAM entities

cards.statement: An IAM policy can authorize access by matching a principal's project tag to a resource's project tag.
cards.explanation: Attribute-based access control can compare principal and resource tags. A shared project value can determine which resources an identity may access.

source.title: Define permissions based on attributes with ABAC authorization

cards.statement: An IAM user group's ARN can identify the Principal in an AWS resource-based policy.
cards.explanation: IAM user groups organize permissions but are not authenticated identities. A resource-based policy cannot name an IAM user group as its Principal.
cards.misconception: An IAM user group can act as an authenticated principal when accessing a resource.

source.title: AWS JSON policy elements: Principal

cards.statement: A customer-specific external ID helps prevent confused-deputy attacks through a third party's IAM role access.
cards.explanation: An external ID condition binds a third party's role-assumption request to the intended customer, reducing the risk of another customer misusing that relationship.

source.title: Access to AWS accounts owned by third parties

cards.statement: A service control policy attached to the organization root restricts IAM users in the management account.
cards.explanation: Service control policies do not restrict principals in the AWS Organizations management account, even when the policy is attached to the organization root.
cards.misconception: Policies attached to the organization root constrain the management account like member accounts.

source.title: Service control policies (SCPs)

cards.statement: An application on Amazon EC2 can retrieve its instance-profile role credentials from instance metadata.
cards.explanation: An instance profile associates an IAM role with an EC2 instance. Applications can use the instance metadata credential provider to obtain that role's credentials.

source.title: Use an IAM role to grant permissions to applications running on Amazon EC2 instances

cards.statement: Security groups permit responses to allowed inbound connections regardless of their outbound rules.
cards.explanation: Security groups track connection state. Response traffic for an allowed inbound connection is permitted even when an outbound rule does not separately allow it.

source.title: Control traffic to your AWS resources using security groups

cards.statement: A network ACL resolves overlapping rules by applying the rule with the most specific matching CIDR.
cards.explanation: Network ACLs evaluate rules in ascending rule-number order. The first matching rule determines whether traffic is allowed or denied.
cards.misconception: Network ACLs use CIDR specificity rather than rule numbers to resolve overlapping rules.

source.title: Control subnet traffic with network access control lists

cards.statement: A public NAT gateway can accept internet-initiated connections to instances in a private subnet.
cards.explanation: A public NAT gateway supports connections initiated from inside the VPC and their responses. It does not provide inbound connection forwarding from the internet.
cards.misconception: A public NAT gateway provides inbound port forwarding to private instances.

source.title: NAT gateways

cards.statement: An interface VPC endpoint reaches a supported AWS service through private IP addresses in selected subnets.
cards.explanation: An interface endpoint creates network interfaces in the selected subnets. Their private IP addresses provide entry points for reaching the supported service.

source.title: Access an AWS service using an interface VPC endpoint

cards.statement: AWS Secrets Manager rotation can update a database password in both the secret and the database.
cards.explanation: Secrets Manager credential rotation coordinates the stored secret with the target database, so the secret reflects a credential accepted by that database.

source.title: Rotate AWS Secrets Manager secrets

cards.statement: An Amazon Cognito user pool exchanges identity-provider tokens for temporary AWS credentials.
cards.explanation: Amazon Cognito identity pools exchange supported identity-provider tokens for temporary AWS credentials. User pools authenticate users and issue application tokens.
cards.misconception: Cognito user pools and identity pools perform the same AWS credential exchange.

source.title: Amazon Cognito identity pools

cards.statement: AWS Shield Advanced protection is automatically included when an AWS account is created.
cards.explanation: AWS Shield Standard provides automatic baseline DDoS protection. Shield Advanced requires a separate subscription for its additional protections and capabilities.
cards.misconception: The automatically included Shield protection is the Advanced tier.

source.title: How AWS Shield and Shield Advanced work

cards.statement: Amazon GuardDuty can block suspicious packets inline as they travel to an Amazon EC2 instance.
cards.explanation: GuardDuty analyzes security signals and generates findings. Blocking traffic requires separate response controls rather than inline packet filtering by GuardDuty.
cards.misconception: Threat detection by GuardDuty includes inline network enforcement.

source.title: Amazon GuardDuty FAQs

cards.statement: An AWS Direct Connect connection encrypts traffic between an on-premises network and AWS by default.
cards.explanation: Direct Connect does not encrypt traffic by default. A design requiring encryption can add a suitable mechanism, such as an IPsec VPN over the connection.
cards.misconception: A dedicated private connection automatically provides transport encryption.

source.title: Encryption in AWS Direct Connect

cards.statement: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager uses outbound HTTPS connections from the managed node for sessions.
cards.explanation: The managed node establishes outbound HTTPS connections to the required Systems Manager endpoints. Its network configuration needs to allow that connectivity.

source.title: Step 1: Complete Session Manager prerequisites

cards.statement: An internet-facing Application Load Balancer can forward requests to targets in private subnets.
cards.explanation: An internet-facing load balancer connects to targets using their private IP addresses. The targets can remain in private subnets while the load balancer accepts internet traffic.

source.title: How Elastic Load Balancing works

cards.statement: Automatic AWS KMS key rotation re-encrypts existing application data with the new key material.
cards.explanation: KMS rotation changes the key material used for new cryptographic operations. Existing ciphertext remains unchanged, and KMS retains older material for decryption.
cards.misconception: Rotating KMS key material also rewrites previously encrypted application data.

source.title: Rotate AWS KMS keys

cards.statement: An Amazon EBS snapshot encrypted with the default AWS managed key can be shared with another AWS account.
cards.explanation: Cross-account sharing of an encrypted EBS snapshot requires a customer managed KMS key. A snapshot encrypted with the default AWS managed key is ineligible.
cards.misconception: The default AWS managed EBS key supports sharing encrypted snapshots across accounts.

source.title: Share an Amazon EBS snapshot with other AWS accounts

cards.statement: Downloading an Amazon S3 object encrypted with SSE-KMS requires kms:Decrypt permission on its KMS key.
cards.explanation: Access to an SSE-KMS object depends on key authorization as well as S3 authorization. The downloader needs permission to decrypt using the object's KMS key.

source.title: Using server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS)

cards.statement: A user with bypass permission can shorten Amazon S3 Object Lock governance-mode retention.
cards.explanation: Bypassing S3 governance retention requires s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission and an explicit x-amz-bypass-governance-retention:true request header.

source.title: Locking objects with Object Lock

cards.statement: An Amazon S3 presigned URL can grant object permissions beyond those held by its signing principal.
cards.explanation: A presigned URL is limited by the signing principal's permissions. The URL cannot authorize an object operation that its signer lacks permission to perform.
cards.misconception: Possessing a presigned URL provides broader object access than the signer can authorize.

source.title: Download and upload objects with presigned URLs

cards.statement: A default DeleteObject request in a versioning-enabled Amazon S3 bucket adds a delete marker.
cards.explanation: When DeleteObject omits a version ID, S3 adds a delete marker instead of erasing stored versions. The earlier object version remains available for recovery.

source.title: Deleting object versions from a versioning-enabled bucket

cards.statement: Configuring Amazon S3 live replication automatically backfills existing objects in the source bucket.
cards.explanation: S3 live replication handles eligible objects written after replication is configured. Existing objects require a separate operation, such as S3 Batch Replication.
cards.misconception: Enabling a live replication rule automatically backfills the source bucket's existing objects.

source.title: Replicating objects within and across Regions

cards.statement: An Amazon RDS DB snapshot can restore an existing DB instance's database contents in place.
cards.explanation: Restoring an RDS DB snapshot creates a new DB instance. Snapshot restoration does not replace the contents of an existing instance in place.
cards.misconception: RDS snapshot restoration is an in-place rollback operation for an existing DB instance.

source.title: Restoring to a DB instance

cards.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket policy can enforce HTTPS by denying requests where aws:SecureTransport is false.
cards.explanation: aws:SecureTransport indicates whether an S3 request uses HTTPS. A bucket-policy Deny conditioned on a false value rejects HTTP requests.

source.title: Examples of Amazon S3 bucket policies

cards.statement: AWS Certificate Manager renews in-use, ACM-issued public certificates with valid public DNS validation records.
cards.explanation: ACM can automatically renew a DNS-validated public certificate used by an AWS service when its required validation CNAME records remain publicly accessible.

source.title: Renewal for domains validated by DNS

cards.statement: Changing a primary AWS KMS multi-Region key's policy automatically updates its replica key policies.
cards.explanation: Related multi-Region KMS keys have independently managed key policies. A policy change on the primary key does not propagate to replica policies.
cards.misconception: Multi-Region KMS keys synchronize access policies along with their shared cryptographic properties.

source.title: How multi-Region keys work

cards.statement: Amazon Macie custom data identifiers can use regular expressions to detect organization-specific sensitive data.
cards.explanation: A Macie custom data identifier describes a sensitive-data pattern with a regular expression. Optional keywords and proximity rules can refine the matches.

source.title: Building custom data identifiers

cards.statement: An Amazon SQS standard queue can redeliver a message even after a successful DeleteMessage call.
cards.explanation: A standard SQS queue can retain a redundant message copy when its storage server is temporarily unavailable during deletion. Idempotent processing protects against that copy arriving later.

source.title: DeleteMessage

cards.statement: An Amazon SQS consumer can permanently remove a message by retrieving it with ReceiveMessage.
cards.explanation: ReceiveMessage retrieves messages and temporarily hides them according to the visibility timeout. DeleteMessage is the separate operation that removes a processed message.
cards.misconception: Reading a message from SQS also acknowledges and deletes it.

source.title: Amazon SQS visibility timeout

cards.statement: An Amazon SQS FIFO queue preserves a single processing order across different message groups.
cards.explanation: An SQS FIFO queue preserves order within a message group. Different groups can be processed concurrently rather than following one queue-wide processing sequence.
cards.misconception: FIFO ordering applies globally across message groups rather than separately within each group.

source.title: Interleaving multiple ordered message groups in Amazon SQS

cards.statement: Separate Amazon SQS subscriptions to an Amazon SNS topic let consumers process their own message copies.
cards.explanation: SNS can send a published notification to multiple subscribed SQS queues. Separate queues let downstream consumers process their copies independently.

source.title: Fanout Amazon SNS notifications to Amazon SQS queues for asynchronous processing

cards.statement: Amazon EventBridge event-bus rules can select events using fields nested inside the event's detail object.
cards.explanation: An EventBridge event pattern can match values within detail, letting a rule select events based on their contents before forwarding them to its targets.

source.title: Creating Amazon EventBridge event patterns

cards.statement: AWS Step Functions Express Workflows can pause for an external worker through task-token callbacks.
cards.explanation: The .waitForTaskToken callback pattern requires a Standard Workflow. Express Workflows do not support that service integration pattern.
cards.misconception: Express and Standard Workflows support the same task-token callback integrations.
cards.volatilityNote: Supported integration patterns for Express Workflows can expand as the service evolves.

source.title: Choosing workflow type in Step Functions

cards.statement: With partial batch responses, AWS Lambda can retry failed SQS records separately from successful records.
cards.explanation: For a Lambda SQS integration, enable ReportBatchItemFailures and return failed message IDs in batchItemFailures. A handled record failure then avoids a whole-batch retry.

source.title: Handling errors for an SQS event source in Lambda

cards.statement: Shared session state in Amazon ElastiCache lets successive user requests reach different application servers.
cards.explanation: Offloading session data to ElastiCache removes the session's dependence on one application server's local memory, allowing other servers to continue that session.

source.title: REL05-BP06 Make systems stateless where possible

cards.statement: Customers patch the underlying host operating system for Amazon ECS tasks running on AWS Fargate.
cards.explanation: AWS Fargate provisions and patches the infrastructure beneath ECS tasks. Customers remain responsible for their container images rather than the underlying host operating system.
cards.misconception: Using ECS on Fargate leaves host operating system patching with the customer.

source.title: AWS shared responsibility model for Amazon ECS

cards.statement: An Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment can serve read queries from its standby.
cards.explanation: The standby in an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment is reserved for failover and does not serve application reads.
cards.misconception: A Multi-AZ DB instance standby also provides read-scaling capacity.

source.title: Multi-AZ DB instance deployments for Amazon RDS

cards.statement: Amazon Aurora's tier-based failover ranking places replica size ahead of configured promotion priority.
cards.explanation: Aurora's tier-based selection favors the highest-priority eligible replica. Instance size breaks ties between replicas with the same priority.
cards.misconception: Aurora ranks replica size ahead of configured promotion priority.

source.title: High availability for Amazon Aurora

cards.statement: Cached DNS answers can delay client switchover during Amazon Route 53 failover.
cards.explanation: DNS resolvers can retain an earlier Route 53 answer until its time to live expires. Failover routing changes do not immediately replace those cached answers.

source.title: Best practices for Amazon Route 53 DNS

cards.statement: A zonal NAT gateway can maintain egress for other Availability Zones during an outage of its own Availability Zone.
cards.explanation: A zonal NAT gateway is redundant only within its Availability Zone. If that zone fails, other zones routing through it lose internet access. Use one zonal NAT gateway per AZ, or a regional NAT gateway.
cards.misconception: A subnet-based NAT gateway's managed redundancy extends across Availability Zones.

source.title: NAT gateway basics

cards.statement: AWS Backup supports copying backups into another AWS account within the same AWS Organizations organization.
cards.explanation: For supported resources, AWS Backup can place a backup copy in another account's vault. The separate copy remains available if the original backup is accidentally deleted.

source.title: Creating backup copies across AWS accounts

cards.statement: A pilot light recovery environment keeps a scaled-down, fully functional application ready to serve traffic.
cards.explanation: Pilot light keeps core services running but requires application resources to be started or deployed during recovery. Warm standby keeps a scaled-down, functional application running.
cards.misconception: Pilot light has the same immediately functional application footprint as warm standby.

source.title: Disaster recovery options in the cloud

cards.statement: A recovery point objective defines the acceptable time needed to restore service after a disaster.
cards.explanation: A recovery point objective specifies acceptable data loss expressed as time. A recovery time objective specifies acceptable service-restoration delay.
cards.misconception: The recovery point objective measures restoration downtime rather than potential data loss.

source.title: REL13-BP01 Define recovery objectives for downtime and data loss

cards.statement: A disaster recovery Region can need higher service quotas before a standby scales to production capacity.
cards.explanation: Recovery Region quotas need to accommodate the workload after failover. Quotas sufficient for a small standby can still prevent it from expanding to production size.

source.title: Disaster recovery options in the cloud

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling can replace capacity in other configured zones when an Availability Zone becomes unavailable.
cards.explanation: A multi-zone Auto Scaling group can launch replacement instances in its healthy configured zones, subject to available capacity, when launches fail in an impaired zone.

source.title: Auto Scaling benefits for application architecture

cards.statement: AWS CloudFormation supports returning a stack to its pre-update configuration after an update fails.
cards.explanation: CloudFormation rollback attempts to return resources to their pre-update configuration. A resource that cannot be restored can interrupt rollback and require intervention.

source.title: Continue rolling back an update

cards.statement: Amazon RDS Proxy drops idle application connections when switching to a replacement writer during failover.
cards.explanation: RDS Proxy preserves idle client connections while reconnecting to the replacement writer. Statements or transactions in progress can still fail.
cards.misconception: Database failover through RDS Proxy requires idle clients to establish new connections.

source.title: RDS Proxy concepts and terminology

cards.statement: An Amazon EBS volume can attach directly to an Amazon EC2 instance in another Availability Zone.
cards.explanation: An EBS volume and the EC2 instance using it must be in the same Availability Zone. Direct volume attachment does not cross that zonal boundary.
cards.misconception: EBS volumes support direct attachment to instances across Availability Zones.

source.title: Amazon EBS volumes

cards.statement: Amazon EBS gp3 volumes support simultaneous attachment to several EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone.
cards.explanation: EBS Multi-Attach supports Provisioned IOPS SSD io1 and io2 volumes, rather than gp3 volumes. Choosing gp3 rules out that shared-block-device configuration.
cards.misconception: The gp3 volume type supports EBS Multi-Attach.
cards.volatilityNote: The volume types eligible for EBS Multi-Attach could expand.

source.title: Attach an EBS volume to multiple EC2 instances using Multi-Attach

cards.statement: Amazon EBS gp3 permits IOPS increases independently of storage-capacity increases.
cards.explanation: With gp3, provisioned performance can be increased separately from storage size, within the volume's supported performance limits.

source.title: Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD volumes

cards.statement: Amazon EBS st1 volumes are tuned for frequent small, random database operations.
cards.explanation: The st1 volume type is designed for large, sequential I/O such as log processing. Small, random database operations are a poor match for this HDD access pattern.
cards.misconception: Throughput-oriented HDD storage suits small, random database I/O.

source.title: Amazon EBS Throughput Optimized HDD and Cold HDD volumes

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 instance store can preserve its data through a stop-and-start cycle of the instance.
cards.explanation: Stopping an EC2 instance discards its instance store data. Data that needs to survive a stop-and-start cycle requires persistent storage elsewhere.
cards.misconception: Instance store data survives an instance stop as long as the instance is later restarted.

source.title: Data persistence for Amazon EC2 instance store volumes

cards.statement: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server can join an existing self-managed Microsoft Active Directory domain.
cards.explanation: An FSx for Windows File Server file system can join a self-managed domain during creation. This supports integration with existing directory identities and resources.
tags: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server

source.title: Using a self-managed Microsoft Active Directory

cards.statement: An Amazon FSx for Lustre file system linked to Amazon S3 can load file contents on first access.
cards.explanation: FSx for Lustre can retrieve a file's contents from its linked S3 repository when first accessed. Preloading needed files avoids that initial retrieval latency.

source.title: Preloading files into your file system

cards.statement: AWS Storage Gateway cached volumes keep their primary data copy on premises.
cards.explanation: Cached volumes keep the primary data in Amazon S3 and retain frequently accessed data locally. The on-premises disks provide a working cache rather than the primary full dataset.
cards.misconception: Cached volumes store the authoritative full dataset locally instead of in Amazon S3.

source.title: How Volume Gateway works

cards.statement: Amazon S3 multipart uploads let an application send different parts of one object in parallel.
cards.explanation: Multipart upload permits concurrent transfers of independent object parts. This lets an application use available bandwidth more effectively for a large upload.

source.title: Uploading and copying objects using multipart upload in Amazon S3

cards.statement: Amazon S3 can return a selected byte range from an object instead of transferring the complete object.
cards.explanation: Byte-range retrieval lets an application fetch the portion of an S3 object it needs. This avoids transferring the remainder when processing part of a large object.

source.title: Performance guidelines for Amazon S3

cards.statement: Amazon EFS Provisioned throughput supports high transfer rates even for file systems storing little data.
cards.explanation: EFS Provisioned throughput is independent of the amount of data stored. A small file system can therefore have throughput provisioned for a demanding workload.

source.title: Amazon EFS performance specifications

cards.statement: Amazon S3 object overwrites use eventual consistency for subsequent reads of the current object.
cards.explanation: S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for successful object overwrites. A subsequent read reflects a completed overwrite rather than an older value awaiting propagation.
cards.misconception: Overwriting an existing S3 object leaves a period of eventual consistency for subsequent reads.

source.title: What is Amazon S3?

cards.statement: Increasing an AWS Lambda function's memory allocation also increases its available CPU power.
cards.explanation: Lambda allocates CPU power in proportion to configured memory. A CPU-bound function can benefit from a memory increase even when its RAM usage is modest.

source.title: Configure Lambda function memory

cards.statement: AWS Lambda reserved concurrency can reduce cold-start latency by pre-initializing execution environments.
cards.explanation: Provisioned concurrency prepares Lambda execution environments ahead of requests. Reserved concurrency reserves and caps concurrency but does not pre-initialize environments.
cards.misconception: Reserving concurrent Lambda executions also keeps execution environments initialized.

source.title: Configuring reserved concurrency for a function

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling target tracking scales CPU capacity by resizing running instances.
cards.explanation: Target tracking adjusts an Auto Scaling group's instance capacity toward a utilization target. It launches or terminates instances instead of resizing running instances.
cards.misconception: EC2 Auto Scaling target tracking changes individual instance sizes to meet a CPU utilization target.

source.title: Target tracking scaling policies for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling can use SQS backlog per instance to scale a queue-processing worker fleet.
cards.explanation: Backlog per instance relates queued work to the workers available to process it. An Auto Scaling policy can use this metric to keep each worker's pending workload near a target.

source.title: Scaling policy based on Amazon SQS

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling can schedule extra capacity before a recurring daily traffic peak.
cards.explanation: Scheduled scaling adjusts an Auto Scaling group's capacity at specified times. Predictable demand can be met in advance rather than after a utilization alarm.

source.title: Scheduled scaling for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling

cards.statement: Amazon ECS Service Auto Scaling directly increases the EC2 instance count to provide room for extra tasks.
cards.explanation: ECS Service Auto Scaling changes the desired task count. If container instances lack resources, extra tasks remain pending until host capacity becomes available.
cards.misconception: Scaling an ECS service directly scales its underlying EC2 host fleet.

source.title: Automatically scale your Amazon ECS service

cards.statement: An Amazon EC2 cluster placement group packs instances into one Availability Zone to reduce inter-instance latency.
cards.explanation: Cluster placement keeps EC2 instances close together within an Availability Zone. This favors tightly coupled workloads that depend on fast communication between instances.

source.title: Placement strategies for your placement groups

cards.statement: An AWS Graviton-based EC2 instance can execute x86-64 application binaries natively.
cards.explanation: Graviton uses the Arm architecture. Native machine-code applications and dependencies need Arm-compatible builds rather than their x86-64 binaries.
cards.misconception: An x86-64 binary can run natively on a Graviton processor unchanged.

source.title: Mixing AWS Graviton with x86 CPUs to optimize cost and resiliency using Amazon EKS

cards.statement: An Elastic Fabric Adapter can bypass the operating system for supported inter-instance communication.
cards.explanation: EFA's operating-system bypass reduces communication overhead for compatible HPC and machine learning libraries, helping tightly coupled workloads exchange data efficiently.

source.title: Elastic Fabric Adapter for AI/ML and HPC workloads on Amazon EC2

cards.statement: A VPC-connected AWS Lambda function can reach the IPv4 internet directly from a public subnet.
cards.explanation: Placing a Lambda function in a public subnet does not give it internet access. IPv4 connectivity needs a suitable egress path, such as a private-subnet route through a NAT gateway.
cards.misconception: A Lambda function acquires direct internet connectivity from a public subnet's internet gateway route.

source.title: Enable internet access for VPC-connected Lambda functions

cards.statement: An Amazon EC2 T3 instance in Standard mode sustains full CPU performance after its CPU credits run out.
cards.explanation: A T3 instance in Standard mode gradually returns to baseline CPU utilization when its accrued credits run out. Sustained bursting requires additional credits.
cards.misconception: Standard-mode T3 instances retain burst-level CPU performance after exhausting their credits.

source.title: Key concepts for burstable performance instances

cards.statement: An AWS Batch array job can run the same containerized workload against many independent input items.
cards.explanation: An array job creates related child jobs from a shared job definition. Each child can process a different input, allowing one submission to coordinate a parallel workload.

source.title: Array jobs

cards.statement: An Amazon RDS read replica can return older data than its source because replication is asynchronous.
cards.explanation: RDS copies source changes to a read replica asynchronously. Applications that read a replica need to tolerate replication lag after a write to the source.

source.title: Working with DB instance read replicas

cards.statement: The Amazon Aurora reader endpoint can spread queries from one connection across multiple reader instances.
cards.explanation: Aurora's reader endpoint balances new connections, not individual queries. Queries sent through an established connection remain on the instance serving that connection.
cards.misconception: The Aurora reader endpoint distributes individual queries rather than database connections.

source.title: Reader endpoints for Amazon Aurora

cards.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB global secondary index can serve strongly consistent reads.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB global secondary indexes support eventually consistent reads. Their query results can lag behind recent changes to the underlying table.
cards.misconception: Strong read consistency can be requested from a global secondary index.
cards.volatilityNote: Supported consistency models for global secondary indexes could expand.

source.title: DynamoDB read consistency

cards.statement: A direct write to Amazon DynamoDB can leave an item cached in DynamoDB Accelerator stale.
cards.explanation: A write that bypasses DAX does not refresh its item cache. Cached data can remain stale until the entry expires, is evicted, or is updated through DAX.

source.title: DAX and DynamoDB consistency models

cards.statement: A result filter on an Amazon DynamoDB query reduces the read capacity consumed by that query.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB applies query filters after reading the matching items. Discarding items from the response does not reduce the capacity consumed to read them.
cards.misconception: A DynamoDB query is charged read capacity based on the items retained after filtering.

source.title: Filter expressions for the Query operation in DynamoDB

cards.statement: Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 can scale an existing DB instance while database transactions are in progress.
cards.explanation: Aurora Serverless v2 adjusts compute capacity within its configured range during active database work. Scaling does not require waiting for transactions to finish.

source.title: How Aurora serverless works

cards.statement: Amazon RDS storage autoscaling reduces allocated storage after large tables are deleted.
cards.explanation: RDS storage autoscaling increases allocated storage but does not shrink it. Deleting table data can free space within the existing allocation rather than reduce that allocation.
cards.misconception: RDS storage autoscaling reverses earlier storage increases when database usage falls.
cards.volatilityNote: Automatic storage scale-down support could change as RDS storage capabilities evolve.

source.title: Managing capacity automatically with Amazon RDS storage autoscaling

cards.statement: AWS DMS data migration tasks can translate stored procedure code for a different database engine.
cards.explanation: DMS replication tasks move data between databases. Converting database code for a different engine is a separate step handled by DMS Schema Conversion.
cards.misconception: The data migration task also converts database procedural code between engines.

source.title: Components of AWS DMS

cards.statement: Amazon Redshift can skip storage blocks when a query filters on a table's sort key.
cards.explanation: Redshift records minimum and maximum column values for storage blocks. Sorting data lets range filters exclude blocks whose values fall outside the requested range.

source.title: Sort keys

cards.statement: A promoted Amazon RDS read replica continues receiving replication updates from its former source.
cards.explanation: Promoting an RDS read replica stops its replication relationship with the source. The promoted database becomes an independent DB instance.
cards.misconception: Read replica promotion preserves incoming replication from the original source.

source.title: Promoting a read replica to be a standalone DB instance

cards.statement: Replacing an AWS Global Accelerator endpoint changes the accelerator's public IP addresses.
cards.explanation: Global Accelerator's static IP addresses remain assigned for the accelerator's lifetime. Changing its endpoints preserves the entry addresses used by clients.
cards.misconception: Changing backend endpoints also changes the accelerator's client-facing IP addresses.

source.title: How AWS Global Accelerator works

cards.statement: Amazon CloudFront Origin Shield can combine simultaneous requests for the same uncached object.
cards.explanation: Origin Shield consolidates requests at an additional cache layer before they reach the origin. Concurrent cache misses for the same object can therefore require fewer origin fetches.

source.title: Use Amazon CloudFront Origin Shield

cards.statement: Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing selects the AWS Region geographically closest to the user.
cards.explanation: Route 53 latency-based routing uses latency measurements between users and AWS Regions. Geographic proximity alone does not determine which Region receives the request.
cards.misconception: Geographic distance is the selection criterion used by latency-based routing.

source.title: Latency-based routing

cards.statement: VPC peering natively routes traffic between two VPCs through a third VPC that is peered with both.
cards.explanation: VPC peering is nontransitive. Two VPCs cannot communicate through a mutual peer merely because each has a peering connection to it.
cards.misconception: Peering relationships can be chained to carry traffic through an intermediate VPC.

source.title: How VPC peering connections work

cards.statement: An AWS Direct Connect gateway can connect an on-premises network to VPCs in multiple AWS Regions.
cards.explanation: A Direct Connect gateway can associate with gateways serving VPCs in different Regions. A single Direct Connect connection can therefore provide access to those VPCs.

source.title: Direct Connect gateways

cards.statement: An AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection provides redundant tunnels to the same customer gateway device.
cards.explanation: The VPN tunnels terminate at separate AWS endpoints. Configuring both on the customer gateway preserves a usable path when a tunnel is unavailable.

source.title: Tunnel options for your AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection

cards.statement: A Network Load Balancer can distribute UDP traffic across its registered application targets.
cards.explanation: Network Load Balancers support UDP listeners and target groups. UDP-based applications can use managed load balancing rather than adding a TCP-only proxy layer.

source.title: Listeners for your Network Load Balancers

cards.statement: An Application Load Balancer can pass a client's encrypted TLS session through to targets for decryption.
cards.explanation: An Application Load Balancer terminates client TLS on its HTTPS listener. HTTPS connections to targets are separate connections rather than the original client TLS session.
cards.misconception: Using HTTPS targets makes an Application Load Balancer a transparent TLS passthrough device.

source.title: Listeners for your Application Load Balancers

cards.statement: AWS Transit Gateway ECMP can combine the bandwidth of multiple VPN tunnels for one TCP flow.
cards.explanation: Transit Gateway distributes VPN traffic across equal-cost paths by flow. One TCP flow uses one tunnel, so aggregate tunnel bandwidth requires multiple flows.
cards.misconception: Equal-cost multipath routing stripes a single TCP flow across several VPN tunnels.

source.title: AWS Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN - AWS Transit Gateway, Single AWS Region

cards.statement: Shared Amazon Route 53 VPC Resolver forwarding rules let multiple VPCs use the same outbound endpoint.
cards.explanation: Sharing a Resolver forwarding rule also shares the outbound endpoint associated with it. VPCs in the same Region can reuse that endpoint for the rule's DNS queries.

source.title: Considerations when creating inbound and outbound endpoints

cards.statement: Amazon CloudFront can forward more request headers to an origin than it includes in the cache key.
cards.explanation: CloudFront separates origin-request forwarding from cache-key composition. A header needed for origin-side analytics can be forwarded without creating extra cache variants.

source.title: Control origin requests with a policy

cards.statement: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams lets consumers replay records that remain within the stream's retention period.
cards.explanation: Kinesis Data Streams retains records after consumers read them. A consumer can revisit retained data, for example to reprocess it after correcting application logic.

source.title: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams FAQs

cards.statement: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams enhanced fan-out gives registered consumers dedicated read throughput per shard.
cards.explanation: Enhanced fan-out consumers receive their own per-shard read throughput. Adding another such consumer does not divide an existing consumer's read allocation.

source.title: Develop enhanced fan-out consumers with dedicated throughput

cards.statement: Amazon Data Firehose can combine incoming records into larger Amazon S3 objects using buffering.
cards.explanation: Firehose buffers incoming records before writing S3 objects. This aggregates records into delivery batches rather than requiring a separate object for each input record.

source.title: Understand data delivery in Amazon Data Firehose

cards.statement: Amazon Data Firehose's built-in format converter can accept CSV input directly for Parquet delivery.
cards.explanation: Firehose's built-in format converter takes JSON input and produces Parquet or ORC. CSV input needs a separate transformation to JSON before using that converter.
cards.misconception: Firehose's native columnar converter accepts CSV as an input format.
cards.volatilityNote: Supported input formats for the built-in converter could expand.

source.title: Convert input data format in Amazon Data Firehose

cards.statement: An AWS Glue crawler can apply detected schema changes to the physical layout of existing source files.
cards.explanation: Glue crawlers infer schemas and update Data Catalog metadata. Changing the underlying source-file contents requires a separate data transformation.
cards.misconception: Updating a catalog schema also transforms the physical files described by that schema.

source.title: Using crawlers to populate the Data Catalog

cards.statement: An Amazon Athena query can reduce scanned data by filtering on a table's partition key.
cards.explanation: Athena can restrict a query to the S3 partitions selected by a partition-key filter. Data in unrelated partitions is skipped instead of scanned.

source.title: Partition your data

cards.statement: Adding task nodes to an Amazon EMR cluster increases the cluster's HDFS storage capacity.
cards.explanation: EMR task nodes contribute processing capacity but do not store HDFS data. Core nodes provide the cluster's HDFS storage.
cards.misconception: Task nodes contribute distributed storage in the same way as core nodes.

source.title: Understand node types in Amazon EMR: primary, core, and task nodes

cards.statement: AWS Lake Formation can restrict queries through integrated engines to selected columns of a data lake table.
cards.explanation: Lake Formation column-level permissions govern which table columns an integrated query engine can return. Analysts can receive access to a subset of a table's data.

source.title: Data filtering and cell-level security in Lake Formation

cards.statement: An AWS Transfer Family SFTP server can write uploaded files directly into an Amazon EFS file system.
cards.explanation: Transfer Family supports EFS as storage for SFTP servers. Existing file-processing applications can work with uploaded data in the associated file system.

source.title: What is AWS Transfer Family?

cards.statement: S3 Standard-IA includes the cost of retrieving object data in its monthly storage charge.
cards.explanation: S3 Standard-IA has a separate data retrieval charge. Frequent access can therefore erode the savings from its lower storage rate.
cards.misconception: The lower Standard-IA storage rate includes data retrieval rather than charging for it separately.
cards.volatilityNote: The separate retrieval-charge policy is part of S3 pricing and could change.

source.title: Understanding and managing Amazon S3 storage classes

cards.statement: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval automatically restores archived data as part of a normal object download request.
cards.explanation: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval needs a separate restore operation before an archived object's data can be downloaded. The application needs to allow for that retrieval delay.
cards.misconception: A normal download request automatically restores archived data instead of requiring a separate restore operation.

source.title: Understanding and managing Amazon S3 storage classes

cards.statement: Amazon S3 lifecycle transitions incur request charges based on the number of objects transitioned.
cards.explanation: S3 charges a transition request per object. For many small objects, transition-request costs can outweigh the storage savings from changing classes.
cards.volatilityNote: The per-object transition charging model is part of S3 pricing and could change.

source.title: Transitioning objects using Amazon S3 Lifecycle

cards.statement: Enabling Requester Pays on an Amazon S3 bucket transfers its object storage charges to the requester.
cards.explanation: With S3 Requester Pays, the bucket owner still pays for stored data. The requester pays the applicable request and download costs instead.
cards.misconception: Requester Pays shifts storage ownership costs along with request and download costs.

source.title: Using Requester Pays general purpose buckets for storage transfers and usage

cards.statement: Successive Amazon EBS snapshots in the standard tier store new and changed blocks incrementally.
cards.explanation: After the first EBS snapshot, subsequent standard-tier snapshots store the blocks changed since the previous snapshot. Unchanged blocks are referenced instead of copied again.

source.title: How Amazon EBS snapshots work

cards.statement: Detaching an Amazon EBS volume pauses its storage charges until it is attached again.
cards.explanation: An EBS volume continues to incur storage charges after detachment. The allocated volume still exists even when an instance is not using it.
cards.misconception: An unattached EBS volume is free because no instance is actively using it.

source.title: Detach an Amazon EBS volume from an Amazon EC2 instance

cards.statement: A file transitioned to Amazon EFS Infrequent Access remains reachable through the same file system path.
cards.explanation: EFS lifecycle management changes a file's storage class while preserving its name and directory structure. Applications keep addressing the file through the existing file system.

source.title: Managing storage lifecycle

cards.statement: An Amazon EBS sc1 volume can serve as the boot volume for an Amazon EC2 instance.
cards.explanation: EBS sc1 volumes do not support boot volumes. A design using sc1 for low-cost data storage still needs a supported root-volume type for the operating system.
cards.misconception: Cold HDD volumes can replace the root volume as well as data volumes.
cards.volatilityNote: The EBS volume types supported as boot volumes could expand.

source.title: Amazon EBS Throughput Optimized HDD and Cold HDD volumes

cards.statement: An Amazon FSx for Lustre scratch file system can lose file data when a file server fails.
cards.explanation: FSx for Lustre scratch deployments do not replicate file data. They trade persistent protection for temporary processing storage suited to data that can be recreated.

source.title: Deployment and storage class options for FSx for Lustre file systems

cards.statement: Restoring an S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval object replaces its archive storage charge with an S3 Standard charge.
cards.explanation: Archive storage charges continue while a restored copy incurs S3 Standard storage charges. Keeping that restored copy longer extends the additional storage billing.
cards.misconception: Restoration substitutes Standard storage billing for archive billing rather than adding a second charge.
cards.volatilityNote: Billing for archived data and restored copies is governed by S3 pricing and could change.

source.title: Transitioning objects using Amazon S3 Lifecycle

cards.statement: AWS Storage Gateway bills virtual tape storage by stored data volume rather than the tape's configured size.
cards.explanation: Tape Gateway storage billing follows the used portion of a virtual tape. Provisioning a larger virtual tape does not itself charge for its unused capacity.

source.title: AWS Storage Gateway FAQs

cards.statement: A Compute Savings Plan can cover eligible Amazon EC2, AWS Fargate, and AWS Lambda usage.
cards.explanation: Compute Savings Plans apply a shared hourly spending commitment across eligible usage of these compute services. A workload can move between them while continuing to use that commitment.

source.title: What are Savings Plans?

cards.statement: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan can follow a workload to the same instance family in another AWS Region.
cards.explanation: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan is tied to a selected instance family and Region. Usage in another Region falls outside that plan's coverage.
cards.misconception: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan is portable between Regions when the instance family stays the same.

source.title: Savings Plans types

cards.statement: A zonal Amazon EC2 Reserved Instance reserves matching instance capacity in its selected Availability Zone.
cards.explanation: A zonal Reserved Instance includes capacity reservation in its chosen Availability Zone. A regional Reserved Instance provides a billing benefit rather than that capacity reservation.

source.title: Regional and zonal Reserved Instances (scope)

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 waits for a running batch job to finish before reclaiming its Spot Instance.
cards.explanation: EC2 can interrupt a Spot Instance while a job is running. Checkpointing progress lets interruption-tolerant jobs resume work instead of starting again from the beginning.
cards.misconception: Running application work protects a Spot Instance from reclamation until the job completes.

source.title: Best practices for Amazon EC2 Spot

cards.statement: An unused portion of an AWS Savings Plans hourly commitment carries forward to cover usage in a later hour.
cards.explanation: Savings Plans commitments apply within each individual hour. An unused amount does not become a credit for a later hour's usage.
cards.misconception: Hourly Savings Plans commitments accumulate as transferable credit when usage is low.

source.title: Understanding how Savings Plans apply to your usage

cards.statement: AWS Fargate calculates a running task's CPU charges from actual CPU utilization rather than allocated vCPUs.
cards.explanation: Fargate compute charges use the task's requested vCPU and memory resources over its billed runtime. Underused allocated CPU still contributes to the bill.
cards.misconception: Fargate meters consumed CPU cycles instead of the CPU resources requested for a task.
cards.volatilityNote: Fargate's resource-based billing model is part of its pricing policy and could change.

source.title: AWS Fargate Pricing

cards.statement: On-demand AWS Lambda invocation duration includes time spent waiting for a synchronous database call.
cards.explanation: An on-demand Lambda invocation accrues duration while its code blocks on a database response. Reducing synchronous waiting can lower the invocation's compute cost.
cards.volatilityNote: The statement concerns on-demand invocation billing; Lambda offers other execution models with different pricing.

source.title: AWS Lambda Pricing

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts support bringing eligible software licenses tied to physical sockets or cores.
cards.explanation: Dedicated Hosts expose physical host information needed for per-socket or per-core licensing. Reusing a license remains subject to its vendor's license terms.

source.title: Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts

cards.statement: Hibernating an Amazon EC2 instance saves its memory contents to the Amazon EBS root volume.
cards.explanation: EC2 hibernation stores RAM contents on the root volume and reloads them when the instance resumes. This can avoid rebuilding an expensive in-memory application state.

source.title: Hibernate your Amazon EC2 instance

cards.statement: An Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling warm pool can keep pre-initialized instances stopped until they are needed.
cards.explanation: A stopped warm pool preserves prepared instances for later scale-out. It reduces the need to keep spare instances running just to avoid lengthy first-time initialization.

source.title: Decrease latency for applications with long boot times using warm pools

cards.statement: EC2 Fleet's price capacity optimized strategy ranks Spot pools by price before evaluating capacity availability.
cards.explanation: EC2 Fleet first identifies pools with high capacity availability, then selects lower-priced pools from that set. Price is evaluated within the capacity-aware selection.
cards.misconception: Price capacity optimized picks the cheapest pools first and considers capacity availability afterward.

source.title: Use allocation strategies to determine how EC2 Fleet or Spot Fleet fulfills Spot and On-Demand capacity

cards.statement: Configuring an AWS Budgets cost alert imposes a hard spending cap at the alert's threshold.
cards.explanation: AWS Budgets alerts notify you about spending rather than capping it. Charges can continue after a notification, so an alert alone does not enforce a spending ceiling.
cards.misconception: Setting a cost alert also prevents the account from accumulating charges beyond its threshold.

source.title: Managing your costs with AWS Budgets

cards.statement: Amazon DynamoDB on-demand bills throughput according to actual read and write requests.
cards.explanation: On-demand capacity charges follow the requests processed rather than a provisioned throughput allocation. Idle read and write capacity adds no throughput charge.

source.title: DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode

cards.statement: A provisioned Amazon DynamoDB table can throttle a sudden traffic spike while auto scaling adds capacity.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB auto scaling reacts to sustained utilization and takes time to change provisioned capacity. A sudden burst can exceed available throughput before that adjustment finishes.

source.title: Managing throughput capacity automatically with DynamoDB auto scaling

cards.statement: Amazon DynamoDB TTL makes an expired item immediately unavailable to application read requests.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB TTL deletes expired items asynchronously. Items awaiting background deletion can remain readable, so applications needing immediate expiry must check expiration themselves.
cards.misconception: TTL expiration immediately removes an item from application access.

source.title: Using time to live (TTL) in DynamoDB

cards.statement: Amazon DynamoDB transactional writes consume the same per-item capacity as ordinary batch writes.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB prepares and commits each transactional write, consuming twice the per-item write capacity of an ordinary batch write. The extra capacity pays for transaction coordination.
cards.misconception: A transactional group of writes has the same capacity cost as ordinary batching.

source.title: DynamoDB read and write operations

cards.statement: An Amazon RDS reserved DB instance for MySQL can discount RDS for PostgreSQL instance usage.
cards.explanation: An RDS reserved DB instance requires a matching database engine for its discount. A MySQL reservation does not cover PostgreSQL usage.
cards.misconception: An RDS reservation discount carries across database engines.

source.title: Reserved DB instances for Amazon RDS

cards.statement: Amazon RDS for SQL Server offers deployments with the SQL Server software license bundled into the service price.
cards.explanation: The RDS for SQL Server License Included model incorporates the SQL Server software license into RDS pricing. A separate SQL Server license purchase is unnecessary for that model.

source.title: Licensing Microsoft SQL Server on Amazon RDS

cards.statement: Aurora I/O-Optimized bills database read and write I/O separately from instance and storage charges.
cards.explanation: Aurora I/O-Optimized has no additional charges for database read and write I/O. Its instance and storage pricing replaces the separate per-I/O billing used by Aurora Standard.
cards.misconception: I/O-Optimized changes performance but preserves separate per-I/O billing.
cards.volatilityNote: The inclusion of read and write I/O in this pricing model could change.

source.title: Amazon Aurora storage

cards.statement: Adding an Aurora Replica within an Amazon Aurora cluster reuses the existing shared database volume.
cards.explanation: An Aurora Replica connects to the cluster's shared storage instead of creating another full copy of the table data. Adding a reader therefore does not duplicate the cluster's database storage.

source.title: Amazon Aurora storage

cards.statement: Deleting an Amazon RDS DB instance automatically removes its previously created manual DB snapshots.
cards.explanation: Manual RDS snapshots survive deletion of their source DB instance. Retaining those snapshots can continue to incur storage charges until they are deleted separately.
cards.misconception: Deleting a database instance also deletes its manual snapshots.

source.title: Deleting a DB instance

cards.statement: AWS DMS can replicate ongoing changes into a target database initially loaded by another tool.
cards.explanation: A DMS change data capture task can follow an existing bulk load. Its source-log starting point must align with that load to avoid gaps or inconsistencies.

source.title: Creating tasks for ongoing replication using AWS DMS

cards.statement: An Amazon RDS reserved DB instance purchase can apply its discount to an already running matching DB instance.
cards.explanation: RDS applies reservation benefits through billing when running usage matches the reservation. The database does not need to be moved to a newly created instance.

source.title: Amazon RDS Reserved Instances

cards.statement: Amazon Redshift Spectrum requires copying an S3 dataset into warehouse tables before querying that dataset.
cards.explanation: Redshift Spectrum queries external data in Amazon S3 directly. Keeping suitable data in S3 avoids loading another copy into Redshift tables for those queries.
cards.misconception: Spectrum requires a warehouse data load before it can query S3 data.

source.title: Amazon Redshift Spectrum

cards.statement: Routing same-Region Amazon S3 traffic through a gateway endpoint avoids NAT gateway data-processing charges.
cards.explanation: An S3 gateway endpoint bypasses the NAT gateway for that traffic. Gateway endpoints also have no hourly or data-processing charge, removing that NAT processing expense.

source.title: Amazon VPC Pricing

cards.statement: An EC2 instance using a zonal NAT gateway in a different Availability Zone incurs no cross-AZ data-transfer charge.
cards.explanation: Traffic from an instance to a NAT gateway in another AZ is billed as cross-AZ data transfer, on top of NAT gateway processing charges. One zonal NAT gateway per AZ avoids it.
cards.misconception: Assuming NAT gateway traffic costs the same whichever Availability Zone the gateway is in.

source.title: Pricing for NAT gateways

cards.statement: An active VPC peering connection incurs an hourly connection fee in addition to applicable data-transfer charges.
cards.explanation: VPC peering has no hourly connection fee. AWS bills applicable traffic rather than time spent maintaining the peering connection.
cards.misconception: VPC peering uses an hourly connection charge like a managed network gateway.
cards.volatilityNote: The absence of a peering connection-hour fee is a pricing policy that could change.

source.title: What is VPC peering?

cards.statement: Amazon S3 charges standard internet data-transfer-out rates when CloudFront fetches objects from an S3 origin.
cards.explanation: Data transferred from Amazon S3 to CloudFront is exempt from S3 data-transfer-out charges. This exemption concerns the origin-to-CloudFront leg, not delivery from CloudFront to viewers.
cards.misconception: An S3 origin fetch is billed as ordinary S3 internet egress.
cards.volatilityNote: The S3-to-CloudFront data-transfer exemption is a pricing policy that could change.

source.title: Amazon S3 pricing

cards.statement: Using private IP addresses makes inter-Region traffic between peered VPCs exempt from data-transfer charges.
cards.explanation: Inter-Region VPC peering carries traffic privately but still incurs inter-Region data-transfer charges. Private addressing does not remove the cost of crossing AWS Regions.
cards.misconception: Traffic is free between Regions when it uses private addresses instead of the internet.
cards.volatilityNote: Inter-Region data-transfer charging policies can change.

source.title: What is VPC peering?

cards.statement: AWS PrivateLink bills an interface endpoint a single regional hourly fee across its deployed Availability Zones.
cards.explanation: PrivateLink endpoint-hour charges apply for each Availability Zone where an interface endpoint is provisioned. Expanding its zonal footprint increases that hourly cost component.
cards.misconception: One regional endpoint-hour fee covers a multi-zone interface endpoint.
cards.volatilityNote: Per-Availability Zone endpoint-hour billing is a pricing policy that could change.

source.title: AWS PrivateLink pricing

cards.statement: AWS Direct Connect port-hour charges depend on provisioned connection capacity rather than actual bandwidth use.
cards.explanation: Direct Connect charges for the selected port capacity over its provisioned lifetime. Reducing traffic through the same provisioned port does not reduce its port-hour rate.
cards.volatilityNote: The provisioned-capacity basis for port-hour pricing could change.

source.title: AWS Direct Connect pricing

cards.statement: Amazon Route 53 waives DNS query charges for alias records that point directly to an Application Load Balancer.
cards.explanation: Queries matching a Route 53 alias record directed to an AWS load balancer are free of DNS query charges. The exemption does not remove the hosted zone's separate cost.
cards.volatilityNote: The query-fee exemption for supported AWS alias targets could change.

source.title: Amazon Route 53 pricing

cards.statement: Selecting a lower Amazon CloudFront price class blocks viewers located outside its included geographies.
cards.explanation: CloudFront price classes select the edge locations used to serve content, not the countries allowed to view it. Viewers outside the selected locations can still receive the content.
cards.misconception: A CloudFront price class is a geographic access restriction.

source.title: Amazon CloudFront pay-as-you-go pricing

cards.statement: A NAT instance's forwarding bandwidth depends on the network capacity of its Amazon EC2 instance type.
cards.explanation: A NAT instance inherits its EC2 instance type's bandwidth limits. Selecting a cheaper instance can reduce the forwarding capacity available to the workloads using it.

source.title: Compare NAT gateways and NAT instances

cards.statement: Enabling cross-zone load balancing on a Network Load Balancer adds no inter-AZ data-transfer charges.
cards.explanation: NLB cross-zone load balancing is off by default; when enabled, inter-AZ data transfer is charged. ALB cross-zone is on by default, and ALB inter-AZ traffic carries no such charge.
cards.misconception: The Application Load Balancer cross-zone fee exemption also applies to Network Load Balancers.

source.title: Elastic Load Balancing FAQs

cards.statement: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration can add data-transfer fees to uploads from the internet.
cards.explanation: Standard S3 internet uploads have no data-transfer-in charge, but accelerated uploads can incur a separate acceleration fee. Faster ingestion can therefore introduce an additional transfer cost.
cards.volatilityNote: Transfer Acceleration surcharges and standard upload transfer pricing could change.

source.title: Amazon S3 pricing
